[[Category:Transformer]]
A '''residual connection''' adds the input of a sub-layer to the output of that sub-layer, so that the sub-layer only has to learn a correction to its input. Both sub-layers of a [[Transformer]] block, [[self-attention]] and the [[Feed-Forward Network (FFN) Sub-Layer (Transformer)|FFN]], are wrapped in a residual connection and a layer normalisation.<ref>{{#cite:Q3130}}{{#cite:Q3269}}</ref>

== Definition ==

Let $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}$ be the input of a sub-layer, and let $\operatorname{SL}$ be the map that sub-layer computes. The '''residual connection''' replaces $\operatorname{SL}$ by

$$
\operatorname{Res}(\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X}+\operatorname{SL}(\mathbf{X}).
$$

The sum is defined only if $\operatorname{SL}$ returns a matrix of the same shape, which is why every sub-layer of a Transformer outputs width $d$.

<blockquote>
With $\operatorname{SL}\equiv\mathbf{0}$ the connection is the identity, $\operatorname{Res}(\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X}$, so a deeper stack can reproduce a shallower model exactly. That is the reason depth does not hurt in principle.<ref>{{#cite:Q3269}}</ref>
</blockquote>

== Layer normalisation ==

'''Layer normalisation''' (LN) normalises the $d$ components of 1 position to zero mean and unit variance, then rescales and shifts them with 2 learned vectors,

$$
\operatorname{LN}(\vec x)
=\vec\gamma\odot\frac{\vec x-\mu\,\mathbf{1}}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2}+\epsilon}}+\vec\beta,
\qquad
\mu=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_i,
\qquad
\sigma^{2}=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left(x_i-\mu\right)^{2},
$$

where $\vec\gamma,\vec\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ are [[model parameters (ANN)|parameters]] (a gain and a bias, $2d$ parameters in total per LN), $\epsilon\approx10^{-5}$ guards the division, and $\odot$ is the elementwise product.<ref>{{#cite:Q3264}}</ref> Applied to a sequence it acts row by row,

$$
\operatorname{LN}(\mathbf{X})
=\begin{pmatrix}
\operatorname{LN}\left(\vec x_1\right)^{\top}\\
\vdots\\
\operatorname{LN}\left(\vec x_T\right)^{\top}
\end{pmatrix},
$$

so the statistics are taken over the features of 1 position. They do not depend on the other examples of the batch, and are the same during training and at inference, which is not the case for batch normalisation.

=== Invariance to shift and scale ===

Setting $\epsilon=0$ for clarity, the mean and the variance of $\alpha\vec x+c\mathbf{1}$ are

$$
\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left(\alpha x_i+c\right)=\alpha\mu+c,
\qquad
\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left(\alpha x_i+c-\alpha\mu-c\right)^{2}=\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2},
$$

hence, for $\alpha>0$,

$$
\operatorname{LN}\left(\alpha\vec x+c\mathbf{1}\right)
=\vec\gamma\odot\frac{\alpha\left(\vec x-\mu\mathbf{1}\right)}{\alpha\sqrt{\sigma^{2}}}+\vec\beta
=\operatorname{LN}\left(\vec x\right).
$$

<blockquote>
So the scale $\alpha$ and the offset $c$ produced by the layer before LN are erased by it, and $\vec\gamma,\vec\beta$ are the only quantities that set the scale and the offset of the normalised output.
</blockquote>

== Gradient path ==

Write the representation after block $l$ as $\mathbf{Y}_l$, so that

$$
\mathbf{Y}_l=\mathbf{Y}_{l-1}+F_l\left(\mathbf{Y}_{l-1}\right),
\qquad l=1,\cdots,L,
\qquad \mathbf{Y}_0=\mathbf{X},
$$

where $F_l$ is the sub-layer of block $l$. Treating $\partial\mathbf{Y}_l/\partial\mathbf{Y}_{l-1}$ as the linear map it induces on the flattened matrix,

$$
\frac{\partial\mathbf{Y}_l}{\partial\mathbf{Y}_{l-1}}
=\mathbf{I}+\frac{\partial F_l}{\partial\mathbf{Y}_{l-1}}
=\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{J}_l,
$$

so by the chain rule the gradient that reaches the input is

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathbf{Y}_0}
=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathbf{Y}_L}\prod_{l=1}^{L}\left(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{J}_l\right).
$$

For $L=2$ the product reads

$$
\left(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{J}_2\right)\left(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{J}_1\right)
=\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{J}_1+\mathbf{J}_2+\mathbf{J}_2\mathbf{J}_1,
$$

and the same holds for general $L$: every product of $k$ Jacobians appears once. In particular the term with $k=0$ is $\mathbf{I}$, so a gradient can travel from block $L$ to block $0$ through the identity alone, without being multiplied by any $\mathbf{J}_l$.

A plain stack has no such term. With $\mathbf{Y}_l=F_l(\mathbf{Y}_{l-1})$,

$$
\frac{\partial\mathbf{Y}_L}{\partial\mathbf{Y}_0}=\prod_{l=1}^{L}\mathbf{J}_l,
\qquad
\left\|\prod_{l=1}^{L}\mathbf{J}_l\right\|\le\kappa^{L}\ \text{ if }\ \left\|\mathbf{J}_l\right\|\le\kappa<1,
$$

which is the vanishing-gradient problem: the factor decays geometrically with depth.

== Placement ==

2 placements are in use. They differ in whether LN sits on the residual path or inside the branch,

{| class="wikitable"
|-
! Post-LN
! Pre-LN
|-
| $\mathbf{X}^{(l+1)}=\operatorname{LN}\left(\mathbf{X}^{(l)}+\operatorname{SL}\left(\mathbf{X}^{(l)}\right)\right)$
| $\mathbf{X}^{(l+1)}=\mathbf{X}^{(l)}+\operatorname{SL}\left(\operatorname{LN}\left(\mathbf{X}^{(l)}\right)\right)$
|}

With $\mathbf{D}_l$ the Jacobian of the LN, the 1-step Jacobians are

$$
\text{Post-LN: }\ \frac{\partial\mathbf{X}^{(l+1)}}{\partial\mathbf{X}^{(l)}}=\mathbf{D}_l\left(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{J}_l\right),
\qquad
\text{Pre-LN: }\ \frac{\partial\mathbf{X}^{(l+1)}}{\partial\mathbf{X}^{(l)}}=\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{J}_l\mathbf{D}_l .
$$

In Post-LN the term of the product that carries no $\mathbf{J}$ is $\prod_{l=1}^{L}\mathbf{D}_l$, so the identity path is rescaled at every layer. In Pre-LN that term is $\mathbf{I}$ itself, and LN acts only inside the branch: the residual stream keeps its scale, and a final LN is applied before the output head, since no block normalises it.

<blockquote>
'''Consequence''': at initialisation Post-LN produces large expected gradients for the parameters near the output, so a large learning rate there is unstable and a warm-up phase is needed; Pre-LN keeps those gradients bounded and trains without a warm-up phase.<ref>{{#cite:Q3281}}</ref> The original Transformer is Post-LN, trained with a warm-up phase.<ref>{{#cite:Q3130}}</ref>
</blockquote>

== Example ==

{{Hidden example}}
'''Setup'''

Let $d=3$, $T=1$, $\vec x=(1,2,3)^{\top}$, $\vec\gamma=\mathbf{1}$, $\vec\beta=\vec 0$, $\epsilon=0$, and let the sub-layer be the cyclic shift

$$
\mathbf{W}=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1&0\\
0&0&1\\
1&0&0
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\operatorname{SL}(\vec x)=\mathbf{W}\vec x .
$$

'''Statistics of the input'''

$$
\mu=2,
\qquad
\sigma^{2}=\frac{(1-2)^{2}+0^{2}+(3-2)^{2}}{3}=\frac{2}{3},
\qquad
\sigma\approx0.8165,
$$

$$
\operatorname{LN}(\vec x)\approx
\begin{pmatrix}
-1.2247\\
0\\
1.2247
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

'''Post-LN'''

$$
\vec x+\operatorname{SL}(\vec x)=
\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}+
\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\1\end{pmatrix}=
\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\\4\end{pmatrix},
$$

with $\mu=4$ and $\sigma^{2}=\frac{2}{3}$, hence

$$
\operatorname{LN}\left(\vec x+\operatorname{SL}(\vec x)\right)\approx
\begin{pmatrix}
-1.2247\\
1.2247\\
0
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

'''Pre-LN'''

$$
\operatorname{SL}\left(\operatorname{LN}(\vec x)\right)\approx
\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
1.2247\\
-1.2247
\end{pmatrix}
$$

so

$$
\vec x+\operatorname{SL}\left(\operatorname{LN}(\vec x)\right)\approx
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
3.2247\\
1.7753
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

'''Gradient through 10 blocks'''

With $\mathbf{J}_l=j\mathbf{I}$ and $j=0.1$,

$$
\begin{cases}
\text{plain stack: } j^{10}=1\cdot10^{-10},\\
\text{with residuals: } \left(1+j\right)^{10}\approx2.59.
\end{cases}
$$

which is the factor that multiplies a gradient on its way from block 10 back to block 0.
{{End hidden}}
